report:
## Conclusion

The best available evidence indicates that **ivermectin does not reduce the risk of death in COVID-19**. Early, smaller studies suggesting mortality benefit were of low quality and low certainty, and have not held up under rigorous testing.

The largest and most rigorous randomized controlled trials—including the TOGETHER trial (NEJM) and ACTIV-6 (JAMA)—found no meaningful clinical benefit of ivermectin for COVID-19 outpatients, including no reduction in hospitalization or disease progression (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMc2207995; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivermectin_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic).

A comprehensive 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 33 RCTs (n=10,489 patients)—the largest and most current pooled analysis—concluded that ivermectin "did not have an effect in reducing the risk of mortality in patients with COVID-19" (https://www.cell.com/heliyon/fulltext/S2405-8440(24)03678-8). A separate 2024 meta-analysis similarly found that while ivermectin might modestly alleviate symptoms, it "did not significantly improve critical clinical outcomes like mortality, ICU admissions, or ventilator use" (https://www.ovid.com/jnls/annals-of-medicine-and-surgery/fulltext/10.1097/ms9.0000000000002762~the-impact-of-ivermectin-on-covid-19-outcomes-a-systematic).

An earlier 2021 meta-analysis had suggested a mortality benefit, but this finding was explicitly rated as based on "low certainty of evidence" (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187140212100206X)—and many of the trials underlying such early optimistic findings were later found to be flawed or fraudulent, contributing to the shift in scientific consensus.

**Bottom line:** Based on the highest-quality, most recent evidence (large RCTs and comprehensive 2024 meta-analyses), ivermectin has not been shown to reduce COVID-19 mortality, and major health authorities do not recommend it for this purpose outside clinical trials.
